marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q019.takeaway: Granulosa cells aromatize theca-derived androgens to estrogens under FSH stimulation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q019.displayText:
Granulosa cells aromatize theca-derived androgens to estrogens under FSH stimulation.

Estrogen are secreted primarily by the granulosa cells of the ovarian follicles, the corpus luteum,
and the placenta .
emphasis: Granulosa cells aromatize theca-derived androgens to estrogens under FSH stimulation

rationales.a: Theca cells mainly produce androgen substrate in response to LH rather than final estrogen.
rationales.c: Leydig cells are testicular androgen-producing cells.
rationales.d: Theca interna synthesizes androgens; granulosa aromatase makes estrogen.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q020.takeaway: The two-cell–two-gonadotropin model assigns LH to theca androgen synthesis and FSH to granulosa aromatization.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q020.displayText:
The two-cell–two-gonadotropin model assigns LH to theca androgen synthesis and FSH to granulosa aromatization.

The two-cell–two-gonadotropin hypothesis:
• Estradiol synthesis requires the contribution of two distinct cell types.
• The theca and granulosa cells within the follicle and the theca-lutein and granulosa-lutein cells within the corpus luteum.
• The follicular theca cells, under the control of LH, produce androgens that diffuse to the follicular granulosa cells, where they are converted to estrogens via an FSH-supported aromatization reaction. The granulosa cells cannot convert progesterone to androstenedione because of the lack of the enzyme 17α-hydroxylase.
emphasis: The two-cell–two-gonadotropin model assigns LH to theca androgen synthesis and FSH to granulosa aromatization

rationales.a: FSH and LH support steroidogenesis rather than inhibit ovarian estrogen/progesterone release.
rationales.c: LH provides androgen substrate, while FSH stimulates aromatase; LH does not inhibit estrogen.
rationales.d: Both hormones act at ovarian cells; this is not a split feedback on hypothalamus versus pituitary.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q021.takeaway: Progesterone suppresses GnRH/LH release through negative feedback in the luteal phase.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q021.displayText:
Progesterone suppresses GnRH/LH release through negative feedback in the luteal phase.

Progesterone inhibits LH secretion.

Actions of progesterone:
• Has negative feedback effects on FSH and LH secretion during the luteal phase.
• Maintains secretory activity of the uterus during the luteal phase.
• Maintains pregnancy.
• Raises the uterine threshold to contractile stimuli during pregnancy, i.e. decreases sensitivity of the uterus to oxytocin.
• Participates in the development of the breasts.
• Increases body temperature.
• It stimulates respiration, and the alveolar PCO₂ in women during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle is lower than that in men.
• Large doses of progesterone produce natriuresis, probably by blocking the action of aldosterone on the kidney.
emphasis: Progesterone suppresses GnRH/LH release through negative feedback in the luteal phase

rationales.a: Progesterone generally reduces, rather than increases, uterine responsiveness to oxytocin.
rationales.c: Progesterone raises basal body temperature after ovulation.
rationales.d: Progesterone promotes secretory transformation, whereas estrogen drives endometrial proliferation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q022.takeaway: Estradiol is the most potent circulating estrogen during reproductive years.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q022.displayText:
Estradiol is the most potent circulating estrogen during reproductive years.

• Estradiol is the most abundant in the reproductive age group and is 12 and 80 times more potent than estrone and estriol respectively.
• The principal sex steroids in females are estrogen, progestin, and androgen. Three estrogens are present in significant quantities—estradiol, estrone, and estriol.
emphasis: Estradiol is the most potent circulating estrogen during reproductive years

rationales.a: Estrone is less potent than estradiol and becomes relatively more prominent after menopause.
rationales.b: Estriol is weaker and is especially associated with pregnancy.
rationales.d: Estradiol is the most potent estrogen, so “none” is incorrect.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q023.takeaway: Estradiol is the predominant plasma estrogen in premenopausal nonpregnant women.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q023.displayText:
Estradiol is the predominant plasma estrogen in premenopausal nonpregnant women.

Estradiol is the predominant estrogen in the plasma of premenopausal non-pregnant women. It is primarily secreted from ovaries.

Estrone is synthesized from dehydroepiandrosterone in adipose tissue stroma. Estrone is the abundant circulating form of estrogen in postmenopausal women.

In pregnancy, the placenta uses dehydroepiandrosterone and its 16 alpha-hydroxyl derivative to form large amounts of estrone and estriol.
emphasis: Estradiol is the predominant plasma estrogen in premenopausal nonpregnant women

rationales.b: Estriol predominates in pregnancy, not in nonpregnant reproductive-age women.
rationales.c: Estrone becomes more prominent after menopause.
rationales.d: Androstenedione is an androgen precursor, not an estrogen.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q024.takeaway: Estrogen inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; claiming it stimulates osteoclasts is false.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q024.displayText:
Estrogen inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; claiming it stimulates osteoclasts is false.

Estrogen does not stimulate osteoclast. Rather it prevents osteoporosis by inhibiting osteoclastic activity.

Actions of Estrogen
• Causes maturation and maintenance of the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina.
• Causes proliferation and development of ovarian granulosa cells.
• Proliferation of endometrium.
• Causes the development of female secondary sex characteristics at puberty.
• Maintains pregnancy.
• Lowers the uterine threshold to contractile stimuli during pregnancy.
• Causes the ductal development of the breasts.
• Has both negative and positive feedback effects on FSH and LH secretion.
• Up-regulates estrogen, LH, and progesterone receptors.
• Increases secretion of angiotensinogen and thyroid binding globulin.
• Epiphyseal closure of long bones.
• Increase libido by acting on the hypothalamus.
• Salt and water retention before menstruation.
• ↓ LDL cholesterol.
• ↑ the local production of NO → vasodilation.
• Inhibit osteoclast, prevent osteoporosis.
emphasis: Estrogen inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption; claiming it stimulates osteoclasts is false

rationales.a: Estrogen supports female secondary sexual characteristics.
rationales.c: Estrogen tends to lower LDL and favor a more favorable lipid profile.
rationales.d: Estrogen increases endothelial nitric oxide signaling.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q025.takeaway: Pubic and axillary hair are androgen-dependent, unlike estrogen-mediated breast, vaginal and endometrial changes.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q025.displayText:
Pubic and axillary hair are androgen-dependent, unlike estrogen-mediated breast, vaginal and endometrial changes.

Pubarche or development of axillary and pubic hair is not due to estrogen. It is due to testosterone (in both the sexes).

Puberty in females:
• Involves the beginning of menstrual cycles (menarche), breast development (thelarche), and an increase in adrenal androgen secretion (adrenarche).
• Estradiol induces the development of secondary sex characteristics, including the breasts and reproductive tract, and increased fat in the hips.
• Estrogens also regulate the growth spurt at puberty, vaginal cornification and cervical mucus production, induce closure of the epiphyses, have a positive effect in maintaining bone formation, and can antagonize the degrading actions of parathyroid hormone on bone.
emphasis: Pubic and axillary hair are androgen-dependent, unlike estrogen-mediated breast, vaginal and endometrial changes

rationales.a: Estrogen stimulates vaginal epithelial maturation and cornification.
rationales.c: Estrogen increases cervical mucus production in the follicular phase.
rationales.d: Estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation and cycle changes contribute to menstruation.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q026.takeaway: Placental syncytiotrophoblast secretes β-hCG early in pregnancy.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q026.displayText:
Placental syncytiotrophoblast secretes β-hCG early in pregnancy.

β HCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast of the placenta.

Some important features of βHCG:
• hCG is a glycoprotein that contains galactose and hexosamine.
• It is produced by the syncytiotrophoblast of the placenta.
• It is made up of α and β subunits.
• hCG-α is identical to the α subunit of LH, FSH, and TSH.
• hCG is primarily luteinizing and luteotropic and has little FSH activity.
• Its presence in early pregnancy in urine is the basis of the various laboratory tests for pregnancy, and it can sometimes be detected in the urine as early as 14 days after conception.
emphasis: Placental syncytiotrophoblast secretes β-hCG early in pregnancy

rationales.a: Ovary does not produce the pregnancy-specific β-hCG signal.
rationales.c: Corpus luteum responds to hCG but is not its source.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q027.takeaway: Progesterone is a C21 steroid derived from cholesterol.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q027.displayText:
Progesterone is a C21 steroid derived from cholesterol.

Progesterone has 21 carbon atoms.
emphasis: Progesterone is a C21 steroid derived from cholesterol

rationales.a: C18 is the steroid carbon number of estrogens.
rationales.c: C20 is not the carbon count of progesterone.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q028.takeaway: Milk ejection is a posterior-pituitary oxytocin reflex; the anterior pituitary is not the neuroendocrine effector.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q028.displayText:
Milk ejection is a posterior-pituitary oxytocin reflex; the anterior pituitary is not the neuroendocrine effector.

The neuroendocrine part of the anterior pituitary is not involved in milk ejection. The posterior pituitary is involved in milk ejection reflex.

The posterior pituitary secretes oxytocin, which is responsible for milk ejection. The anterior pituitary produces prolactin, which is responsible for lactogenesis.
emphasis: Milk ejection is a posterior-pituitary oxytocin reflex; the anterior pituitary is not the neuroendocrine effector

rationales.b: Milk is ejected when myoepithelial cells around alveoli/ducts contract; the source’s sinus wording refers to milk movement rather than the endocrine trigger.
rationales.d: Emotional state can modulate the oxytocin milk-ejection reflex.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q029.takeaway: Oxytocin contracts mammary myoepithelial cells to eject milk; prolactin supports milk synthesis.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q029.displayText:
Oxytocin contracts mammary myoepithelial cells to eject milk; prolactin supports milk synthesis.

• Oxytocin causes contraction of the myoepithelial cells lining the mammary ducts and ejects milk during suckling. But, it has no galactogenic effect.
• Prolactin is responsible for milk secretion.
• Estrogens are primarily responsible for the proliferation of the mammary ducts and progesterone for the development of lobules.
emphasis: Oxytocin contracts mammary myoepithelial cells to eject milk; prolactin supports milk synthesis

rationales.a: Prolactin drives milk production, not ejection.
rationales.c: Progesterone supports pregnancy and breast development but does not trigger milk let-down.
rationales.d: FSH regulates ovarian follicular development, not milk release.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q030.takeaway: Oxytocin triggers milk ejection, uterine contraction and myoepithelial contraction; lactogenesis is primarily prolactin-mediated.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH42_Q030.displayText:
Oxytocin triggers milk ejection, uterine contraction and myoepithelial contraction; lactogenesis is primarily prolactin-mediated.

Lactogenesis is not a function of oxytocin. It is caused by prolactin.
emphasis: Oxytocin triggers milk ejection, uterine contraction and myoepithelial contraction; lactogenesis is primarily prolactin-mediated

rationales.b: Milk ejection is a principal oxytocin effect.
rationales.d: Myoepithelial cells contract in response to oxytocin to release milk.
